clue.text: Couple needing space after sex

parts.note: 'it' is a coy old word for sex or sex appeal
an em is a printer's space, the width of a letter M

explanation.surface: A couple who, after making love, want some room to themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' only orders the pieces: the space follows the sex.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a romantically linked pair, as in gossip columns saying two celebrities are now an item.

clue.text: Go and sweet talk leaders in private meeting

parts.note: to have a go is to try

indicators.note: the leaders of a phrase are the letters at the front of each of its words

parts.note: opening letters of both words

explanation.surface: Sweet-talking someone into a secret rendezvous.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a secret meeting arranged between lovers, a private appointment.

clue.text: Low singer shows bum

parts.note: to low is to make the sound a cow makes
Cher, the American pop singer

explanation.surface: A deep-voiced singer mooning the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like an adjective for a bass singer, but it is the cow's verb; 'bum' is not the backside but a scrounger.
explanation.definitionFit: A bum in the American sense is a loafer who cadges from others, and a moocher scrounges in exactly that way.

clue.text: Sailor repeatedly missing love's foremost pleasure

indicators.note: missing means going without, and repeatedly says it happens twice over

parts.note: a Jolly is naval slang for a Royal Marine

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: initial letter of love

explanation.surface: A sailor who keeps missing out on love's chief pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: JOLLY loses both its Ls to leave JOY; a Jolly is Royal Navy slang for a Royal Marine, a seagoing soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Joy and pleasure are close synonyms, both naming a feeling of delight or happiness.

clue.text: Travels without pot for bouncing babies?

indicators.note: something without a thing lacks it, so those letters come out

parts.note: journeys as a verb means travels
an urn is a vase or pot

explanation.surface: Travelling light without a potty for the healthy babies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bouncing babies' suggests healthy infants; the question mark warns they are kangaroos, which hop.
explanation.definitionFit: A joey is a baby kangaroo, and kangaroos famously move by hopping, so the babies literally bounce.

clue.text: PM raised Jamaican fare

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word lifts it so it reads from the bottom upward

parts.note: Theresa May, British Prime Minister when this puzzle appeared

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister bringing up Caribbean food.
explanation.definitionFit: The yam is a starchy tuber that is a staple ingredient in Jamaican cooking, so typical food there.

clue.text: Perhaps the editor is the best setter?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the boss, of whom an editor is one example
second meaning, read literally: the finest of the setter breed of hound

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about whether the crossword editor outranks the puzzle setters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' looks like a crossword compiler, but it is the gundog breed; the question mark flags the editor as only one example of a boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Top dog is an idiom for the person in charge, and literally describes the leading hound among setters.

clue.text: School of Rock admitting primarily undiscovered talent

indicators.note: something admitting another lets it inside itself

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives only its opening letter

parts.note: opening letters of both words

explanation.surface: The film School of Rock, about a fake teacher who finds hidden musical talent in his pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School of Rock' reads as the film title, but 'School' is the verb defining the answer and 'of' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach or train them, which is what a tutor does as a verb.

clue.text: Nearly perfect invention for all to see in favourite haunt

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: pure in the sense of flawless
a lie is a made-up story
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, suitable for everyone

explanation.surface: A nearly flawless invention displayed in someone's favourite spot.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film classification meaning anyone may watch.
explanation.definitionFit: A purlieu is a place where someone habitually goes, their usual stamping ground or regular haunt.

clue.text: Normally one covers a desecrated grave

indicators.note: a thing that covers another goes round the outside of it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something desecrated is violated and disturbed, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Typically someone ends up covering a vandalised grave.
explanation.definitionFit: On average is an idiom meaning usually or as a rule, the same sense as normally.

clue.text: Former playgirl's heart goes to single bishop first

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central part, its middle letters

parts.note: the two central letters of the eight-letter word
single means one

explanation.surface: A playgirl's affections pass to an unmarried bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' puts the bishop at the front, ahead of the heart and the single.
explanation.definitionFit: Bygone describes something belonging to the past, as former does, as in bygone days.

clue.text: After second carrot pie, honk in this?

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second

indicators.note: pie is printer's slang for type spilled into a jumbled heap

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who, after a second slice of carrot cake, might be honking in the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' sounds like time passing after the pie, but it just puts the second first; the question mark makes the definition an example, since you honk a horn in a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A car has a horn that the driver sounds, so a vehicle is somewhere you honk.

clue.text: Some budget changes make a deep impression

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only a part of it, a run of letters inside

parts.note: the run spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A few changes in the budget leave their mark on the economy.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to cut lines into a surface with acid or a tool, a literal deep impression.

clue.text: Comparatively cautious judge to retire after appeal

parts.note: SA is short for sex appeal

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a referee judges a match

explanation.surface: A cautious judge chooses to retire once an appeal is lodged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appeal' looks legal but means sex appeal, abbreviated SA.
explanation.definitionFit: Safer is the comparative of safe, meaning more careful and taking fewer risks.

clue.text: Lacking one flatiron for bashing of one's forehead?

indicators.note: a bashing knocks something out of shape, so the letters are battered into a new order
lacking means without, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flatiron used to bash someone on the forehead.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an iron striking a head; the question mark marks the definition as loose, since frontal refers to the front of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: The frontal bone forms the forehead, so frontal is the anatomical adjective for that part of the skull.

clue.text: Almost perfect vision

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off

parts.note: ideal means perfect

explanation.surface: Eyesight that is nearly twenty-twenty.
explanation.definitionFit: A vision can be a mental picture or conception of something, which is what an idea is.

clue.text: Dutch arranges to employ cleaner

indicators.note: to employ something is to take it on and hold it, so the run of words holds the answer

parts.note: the last two letters of the name plus the first two of the verb

explanation.surface: The setter, Dutch, sorts out hiring someone to clean the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Dutch is the setter's own name, inviting you to treat it as a reference to the compiler; a char is British slang for a cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A char, short for charwoman, is a woman employed to clean someone's house or office.

clue.text: Getting healthier erections?

parts.note: surface reading: a suggestive remark about improved sexual performance
setter's reading: erections are things erected, buildings, and these are where patients get better

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about improving one's sex life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erections' is the trap: here it means structures put up, and 'Getting healthier' describes what goes on inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hospitals are buildings erected for treating the sick so they recover, places for getting well.

clue.text: Oh no — Trump, a "Stormy" kind of guy

indicators.note: something stormy is turbulent and tossed about, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, with the article included

explanation.surface: A groan at Donald Trump, whose scandal involved the adult-film actress Stormy Daniels.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks point at Stormy Daniels, but the word is the anagram signal; a protohuman is an early primitive ancestor, a dig at Trump.
explanation.definitionFit: A protohuman is an early hominid ancestor of modern people, so a sort of man or primitive bloke.

clue.text: Speaker's first to plant a seed

indicators.note: what a speaker says is heard, so the word is spelt by its sound
first picks out only the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: the letter name said out loud; the same letters sitting inside Speaker's is a coincidence

explanation.surface: The Commons Speaker being first to plant a seed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaker' looks like the Commons official, but it signals that the letter is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: A pea is the round edible seed of the pea plant, found in pods.

clue.text: Person with unlimited cash

indicators.note: with no limits means without its boundary letters at either end

parts.note: cash is money

explanation.surface: Someone with limitless money in the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlimited' looks like describing great wealth, but it strips the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: One is used as a pronoun for a person in general, as in one does one's best.

clue.text: Highly seasoned?

parts.note: surface reading: food spiced strongly
setter's reading: seasoned means aged by many seasons, and highly points to lofty raised ground

explanation.surface: Seems to describe a very spicy dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seasoned' suggests salt and pepper, but it means having lived through many seasons; 'Highly' hints at something elevated in the landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for extremely ancient, and the elevated landforms named in it are both lofty and very old.

clue.text: Compared new Kindle with earliest of e-readers

indicators.note: a new version of something is remade, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the earliest of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: opening letter

explanation.surface: A review comparing the latest Kindle with the first electronic reading devices.
explanation.walkthrough: A Kindle is Amazon's e-reader, so the surface fits; 'new' is the anagram signal, not a product launch.
explanation.definitionFit: To liken one thing to another is to compare them, pointing out a resemblance.

clue.text: Getting on in prison without cocaine

indicators.note: without means lacking, so that letter is removed

parts.note: caged means locked up
C is drug slang for cocaine

explanation.surface: Coping in jail without access to drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' looks like managing, but it means growing old.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting on is an idiom for growing old, and aged describes someone who is elderly.

clue.text: Dated soldier, drinking nice bubbly

indicators.note: drinking something takes it inside

parts.note: a soldier ant is a worker caste

indicators.note: bubbly is fizzy and effervescent, so the letters are agitated into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned soldier sipping some pleasant champagne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bubbly' pretends to be champagne the soldier drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient means very old, and dated describes something old-fashioned or out of date.

clue.text: Married type finds squeeze

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
ilk means kind or type

explanation.surface: A married sort who finds himself a new squeeze, or lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squeeze' looks like the slang for a girlfriend, but it is a verb: to milk is to squeeze teats, or to exploit.
explanation.definitionFit: Milking a cow means squeezing the udder, and to milk someone is to squeeze money out of them.

clue.text: See 19
Successes penning new clues

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, as animals are shut inside a pen

parts.note: hits are successes
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A writer's successes come from penning fresh clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Hints are clues, small pieces of information that help someone work something out.

clue.text: One who gets sentimental old fellow into messy place

indicators.note: putting something into a place sets it inside that place

parts.note: a sty, where pigs live, is a byword for mess
O is the abbreviation for old
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: An emotional person bundling an elderly man into a messy room.
explanation.definitionFit: A softy is a soft-hearted person easily moved to tears or sentiment.

clue.text: Dutch will join automobile club, maybe

parts.note: a car is an automobile
D is the abbreviation for Dutch

explanation.surface: The setter, Dutch, signs up to a motoring club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'automobile club' reads like the AA, but 'club' is the playing-card suit and 'maybe' says it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A club is one of the four suits, so any club in a pack is an example of a playing card.

clue.text: Artist not about to sell out

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician

indicators.note: about suggests turning around, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An artist who refuses to sell out for commercial success.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a member of the Royal Academy, is the usual crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat on someone is to betray or inform on them, which is selling them out.

clue.text: Wishes to squander year's income

indicators.note: squandering something means losing it through waste, so it is taken away

parts.note: yearnings are longings or wishes
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: Wanting to blow a whole year's pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'year's income' reads together, but 'year's' belongs to the wordplay and only income is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnings are the money someone receives from work, their income or pay.

clue.text: Blubber smells revolting

indicators.note: revolting means turning over, so the word turns upside down in this down light

parts.note: BO is body odour, a smell; here in the plural

explanation.surface: Whale fat stinks horribly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blubber' is not whale fat but the verb to weep noisily; 'revolting' is not disgusting but rising up.
explanation.definitionFit: To blubber is to cry noisily, and to sob means to weep with convulsive gasps.

clue.text: Party justifies targets to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only a part of the following words is used

parts.note: the tail of the verb runs into the head of the noun

explanation.surface: A political party partly justifies its targets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political, but it is a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiesta is a festive celebration, particularly in Spanish-speaking countries, so a party.

clue.text: Comments made to House while covering face

indicators.note: something covering another wraps round it on the outside

parts.note: as in the sense of while
a face of a solid is one of its sides

explanation.surface: An MP's remarks to the House of Commons made while covering his face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' suggests Parliament, but it is a theatre audience, to whom actors deliver remarks unheard by the other characters.
explanation.definitionFit: On stage, an aside is a remark spoken to the audience, the house, that other characters supposedly cannot hear.

clue.text: Young man's close to comprehending love

indicators.note: comprehending in its old sense means including or taking in

parts.note: by means near or close to
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A young man is close to understanding what love is.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy is a male child or youth, so a young man.

clue.text: Mind being described as XXXL

parts.note: a size label of this kind belongs on a T-shirt
the largest size, at the far end of the range

explanation.surface: Someone's mind called extra-extra-extra large, a huge intellect.
explanation.walkthrough: XXXL is the last size on a T-shirt size chart, so it is the T end; the surface pictures a giant brain.
explanation.definitionFit: To mind something is to look after it, and to tend has the same caretaking sense, as in tending sheep.
